newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada plans sweeping new tobacco restrictions.
newsitem.headline: Canada plans sweeping new tobacco restrictions.

text.p: Canadian Health Minister David Dingwall announced on Thursday sweeping new measures the government plans to introduce to counter the use of tobacco, especially among youth.

The government package, responding in part to a Supreme Court of Canada decision in September 1995 striking down a ban on tobacco ads on the grounds of freedom of speech, would ban tobacco advertising on radio, television or billboards.
It would allow tobacco ads in magazines and newspapers with primarily adult readership.
The legislation, to be introduced in December, would ban sales of tobacco products through vending machines, self-service displays and mail-order sales.
"The need for action is clear. Seven million Canadians are currently victims of tobacco addiction," he told a news conference.

The proposed legislation, likely to pass since Dingwall's Liberal government commands a solid majority in the House of Commons, would also restrict the use of tobacco brand names in sporting, music and other sponsored events.
But the tobacco companies will be allowed to put brand names on the bottom 10 percent of ads and direct mailings.
"Tobacco will cause the deaths of more than 40,000 Canadians this year -- three times the number who will die from car accidents, suicides, drug abuse, murder and AIDS combined," Dingwall said.
Manufacturers will be required to include additional information about the toxic substances in tobacco products and their health impacts on tobacco packaging.
The legislation will "give the government the authority to regulate the constituents of tobacco smoke and tobacco products, such as nicotine," Dingwall said.
Asked if the government would consider limiting nicotine content in the future, he replied: "As the evidence warrants, yes."
The Canadian minister also said he would allocate C$50 million over the next five years to enforce the legislation and support health education programming.
Dingwall said an anti-smuggling plan introduced in 1994 would be continued, and he referred to the previously announced hike in tobacco taxes in much of Canada.

"Together these measures are an important part of our approach to deter tobacco use by gradually increasing the price of cigarettes without causing a return to the serious smuggling problem that precipitated the 1994 tobacco tax reduction," he added.
The three major players in the Canadian tobacco market are:
- Imperial Tobacco Ltd, a unit of Imasco Ltd, which controls about 65 percent of the Canadian cigarette market. Imasco is 40 percent owned by B.A.T. Industries Plc of Britain.
- Rothmans, Benson and Hedges Inc, owned 60 percent by Rothmans International, a unit of Rothmans International Plc, and 40 percent by Philip Morris Cos Inc.
- RJR MacDonald, wholly owned by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp unit R.J. Reynolds Tobacco International.
